sense: of a crime, a wrong, an accident

terms.gloss: the one who has been wronged
terms.grammar: phrase: a relative clause with injūria, injūriae f. and accipiō
evidence: Cic. Div. Caec. 60: injūriam accipere ab aliquō (Lewis & Short, s.v. injūria)
terms.comment: Classical Latin has no single word for the victim of a crime: it names the person by what was done, in a relative clause or a participle: is cui injūria facta est, quī spoliātus est (robbed), quī circumventus est (cheated), quī in eō cāsū periērunt (the victims of an accident).

evidence: Cic. Fin. 2.61: sē victimam reī pūblicae praebēre
terms.comment: Classically an animal offered in sacrifice, and figuratively someone who gives himself up as an offering (Cic. Fin. 2.61). Using it for the victim of a crime or an accident follows the modern languages.

phrases.english: What have they done to you?

sources: Lewis & Short: injuria · Lewis & Short: victima
